You want to know what happened with Parveen? Fine, Bhaijaan, I'll tell you, but don't give me that "Imran, what did you do" look.
I told Faizan about her mum's hospital visits. I don't even know why. He was talking about his own stuff and it just came out. Then it went round the whole class.
When Parveen confronted me, the first thing I said was, "You're overreacting, it's not that big a deal." I actually said that. She just looked at me and walked away, and I got this hot, horrible feeling, like being caught twice.
I didn't sleep. Next day I found her by the cycle stand and said, "I told Faizan. It was wrong. I'm ashamed of it, and you weren't overreacting." I didn't add a "but". I wanted to, so badly.
She didn't forgive me. She said, "Okay. I heard you." That's it. But it felt different from before.

qa.q: Where did Imran find Parveen the next day?
qa.a: Imran found Parveen by the cycle stand.

qa.q: What did Imran feel after saying 'You're overreacting'?
qa.a: Imran got a hot, horrible feeling, like being caught twice, because deflecting made the wrong worse.

qa.q: What made Imran's second attempt a real reckoning?
qa.a: Imran named the act, called it wrong, admitted shame and said Parveen wasn't overreacting, without adding a 'but' to shift the blame.

qa.q: How might Parveen have heard 'You're overreacting' compared with the later apology?
qa.a: The first made Parveen feel blamed for her own hurt; the second didn't fix things, but let her feel heard, which is why she said 'I heard you'.

grounding: Shows a teen who first deflects with 'you're overreacting' and then gives a real apology that names the act without blaming the hurt friend.

I'm Yamini, and my little brother Vaibhav is fifteen. On Thursday his best friend Dhruv came to our door, which he never does without messaging first. I was in the kitchen and heard most of it.
Dhruv said quietly, "You told Neel about my speech classes."
Vaibhav's first answer was, "Bro, relax, it was a joke, you're making it a whole thing." Dhruv didn't say anything. He just started putting his shoes back on.
Then Vaibhav said, "Wait." There was a long pause. I think he was trying to find the words. "I did tell Neel. It was wrong. I wanted everyone to laugh. I'm really ashamed."
Dhruv stopped with one shoe on. I couldn't see his face. After a minute he said, "Okay," and they sat on the steps for a while without talking.
I don't know what either of them felt. I just know that "wait" changed something.

qa.q: What did Dhruv say Vaibhav told Neel about?
qa.a: Dhruv said Vaibhav told Neel about his speech classes.

qa.q: What does the long pause before 'I did tell Neel' suggest about Vaibhav?
qa.a: It suggests Vaibhav was torn between defending himself and facing what he did, and was searching for honest words.

qa.q: Which of Vaibhav's two answers helped, and why?
qa.a: The second: it named what he did, called it wrong and admitted shame, instead of treating Dhruv's hurt as 'a whole thing'.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have felt while putting his shoes back on?
qa.a: Dhruv probably felt dismissed and ready to give up on the friendship, since 'you're making it a whole thing' blamed him for being hurt.

grounding: Illustrates, through an older sibling's eyes, a teen moving from the excuse 'you're making it a whole thing' to owning the act and his shame.

Avni found Lakshmi at the bus stop outside their Kolkata school, alone, earphones in. Avni had rehearsed a dozen versions on the way. Most began with "I didn't mean to" or "It just came out."

She threw all of them away.

"Lakshmi. Can I say something? You don't have to answer."

Lakshmi took one earphone out, her face blank.

"I told Rinku's group about your mother's surgery. I did it because I wanted them to think I was interesting. It was wrong. You trusted me and I used it. I'm ashamed of it."

Lakshmi stared at the road. "Why are you telling me this now?"

"Because you should hear it from me, not them. And I'm not going to say you're overreacting. You're not."

The bus came. Lakshmi didn't get on. She didn't forgive Avni either. But she didn't walk away.

qa.q: Where did Avni find Lakshmi?
qa.a: At the bus stop outside their Kolkata school.

qa.q: Why did Avni throw away the versions that began with "I didn't mean to"?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and wanted to take real responsibility, knowing those openings would sound like excuses.

qa.q: Which part of Avni's apology matters most, and why?
qa.a: Saying plainly what she did and why, and that Lakshmi is not overreacting, because it names the act without blaming Lakshmi for being hurt.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel as she lets the bus go?
qa.a: She is still hurt and wary, not ready to forgive, but perhaps a little relieved that Avni owned it honestly.

grounding: Avni names her betrayal of Lakshmi plainly and admits shame instead of deflecting, showing a real reckoning that doesn't blame the hurt person.

"Rashmi, come on. It was one comment. You're overreacting."

"I'm overreacting? Tanvir, you told the whole cricket team I still sleep with a night light."

"It was a joke. Everyone laughed."

"Exactly. Everyone laughed."

"...Okay, but you didn't have to stop talking to me for a week."

"Yes, I did."

"So now it's all my fault?"

"It is your fault. That's the point."

Silence.

"...Fine. Wait. Let me say it properly."

"Go on."

"I told them because Varun was calling me a mama's boy and I wanted to make them laugh at someone else. I picked you. It was wrong. I'm... actually really ashamed."

"Why didn't you say that a week ago?"

"Because saying you're overreacting was easier than saying I was a coward."

"...That one I believe."

qa.q: What did Tanvir tell the cricket team about Rashmi?
qa.a: That Rashmi still sleeps with a night light.

qa.q: What does Tanvir's switch to "Let me say it properly" show about his feelings?
qa.a: It shows he is ashamed underneath his defensiveness and finally willing to face what he did instead of blaming Rashmi.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Tanvir deflected with "you're overreacting", which blamed Rashmi for her hurt; naming the act, his reason and his shame is what fixed it.

qa.q: How does Rashmi hear "You're overreacting"?
qa.a: She hears it as Tanvir making her the problem, which adds to her hurt and anger.

grounding: Tanvir first deflects with "you're overreacting" and then names his betrayal and shame, showing the difference between an excuse and real accountability.

The first time Arnab confronted me, I said he was making a big deal out of nothing. I actually said that. He had told me about his parents' fights, and I'd repeated it to Sid and Joel on the bus, to sound like I knew things.

Arnab looked at me like I'd slapped him, and walked off.

For two days I told myself he was being dramatic. Then my sister asked why I was sulking, and when I explained, she said, "So he's hurting and you called it drama?"

That stuck.

On Monday I found Arnab by the cycle stand. I said, "I told Sid and Joel about your parents. I wanted to seem interesting. It was wrong, and I'm ashamed. You weren't overreacting."

He didn't say much. He nodded once. But he waited while I unlocked my cycle, and we walked out of the gate together.

— Uday

qa.q: Where did Uday find Arnab on Monday?
qa.a: By the cycle stand.

qa.q: How did Uday feel when his sister asked, "So he's hurting and you called it drama?"
qa.a: Uday felt uncomfortable and ashamed, seeing that calling it drama had blamed Arnab for his own hurt.

qa.q: What did Uday change in his second attempt?
qa.a: He named what he did and why, said it was wrong and that he was ashamed, and told Arnab he wasn't overreacting.

qa.q: What might Arnab have felt when he waited at the cycle stand?
qa.a: He may have felt a cautious relief, still hurt but willing to believe Uday this time.

grounding: Uday first deflects his betrayal as Arnab overreacting, then gives a real apology that names the act without blaming Arnab for his hurt.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 9, Thursday.

Met Aadhya and Farida together, at Farida's request, after Aadhya shared Farida's private message with the class group.

Aadhya began by saying, "It was a joke. Farida's overreacting. Everyone shares screenshots." Farida's face shut down.

I asked Aadhya to look at Farida and describe what she did, just the facts. There was a long silence. Then Aadhya's voice changed. "I took a screenshot of something you told only me. I sent it to thirty people. It was wrong." She stopped, then added, "I'm ashamed. I don't know why I did it."

Farida said nothing for a moment. Then she said, "That's the first time you haven't made it my fault."

Neither was ready to be friends again today. Agreed next step: Aadhya will ask the class group to delete the screenshot, and we'll meet again in a week.

qa.q: How many people did Aadhya send the screenshot to?
qa.a: Aadhya sent it to thirty people.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when her voice changed?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, finally facing what she had done instead of hiding behind 'it was a joke'.

qa.q: Why did the second answer work better than the first?
qa.a: Naming the act as wrong, without calling Farida oversensitive, took real responsibility and made Farida feel heard.

qa.q: How did Farida react to Aadhya's real apology?
qa.a: Farida seemed to feel acknowledged, saying it was the first time Aadhya hadn't blamed her, though she wasn't ready to be friends yet.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teen move from 'you're overreacting' to naming what she did as wrong and admitting shame.
